transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 74 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jenna Ortiz (Redwood SE), Alex Rivers (Heliodor, ML Eng), Priya Nair (Heliodor, Infra), Marcus Li (Heliodor CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
High-level deep dive into per-model tuning for Heliodor's mixed Llama/Mistral/Qwen workload. Focus on MoE routing cost tradeoffs, ROPE scaling/drift with long context, KV cache prewarm strategies for short bursts, and quantization profiles (4-bit vs 8-bit) under Heliodor's throughput SLOs. Decided to run a 2-week Dedicated trial with kernel-level traces and shared prompt set. Next steps and owners captured at end.

Topics covered:
- Baseline latency and throughput expectations for open models (Llama family, Mistral-X variants, Qwen mix)
- MoE routing costs and token affinity strategies to reduce cross-GPU routing
- ROPE decay/scale effects for long-context (tokens > 8k) in retrieval-augmented scenarios
- KV cache prewarm and shared-prefix caching ideas to speed tail latency for chat sessions
- Quantization experiments: Q4 vs Q8 and impact on generation quality for comms use-case
- VPC/on-prem constraints: KMS, firewall, egress, and Dedicated capacity sizing

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for carving time right after the holidays, we'll try to keep this practical, Jenna and I can jump into the perf numbers, alex, priya, marcus, feel free to stop us anytime
[00:15] Alex (Heliodor): yeah thanks, we've got a bunch of open questions—mainly around costs if we use MoE routing for routing personalization, and how ROPE behaves with our long docs, so excited to see the numbers
[00:32] Jenna (Redwood): perfect, quick agenda: 1) baseline perf across your model set, 2) routing/affinity patterns, 3) rope/kv/quant experiments, 4) infra constraints and trial plan
[01:05] Priya (Heliodor): one operational thing — our infra team prefers VPC peering rather than public egress, and we use customer-managed KMS for key rotations, if that's a blocker let us know
[01:30] Samir: not a blocker; Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and VPC peering for Dedicated — we'll need the peering CIDRs and a short firewall matrix, we can share our onboarding checklist
[02:12] Jenna: ok jumping into the first benchmark — we ran synthetic microbenchmarks on three model families with a 32-token prompt and 128-token generation to get steady-state per-token latency. Llama-2-13B baseline on A100 style nodes: ~28 ms/token single-threaded, with static batching of 8 brings effective latency to ~18 ms/token but increases p99 slightly
[02:45] Alex: are those numbers with KV cache warm? our chat flows often have 2-3 message history so warm cache matters
[03:02] Jenna: good call — those are cold-KV numbers. Warm KV with prefix caching drops per-token to ~12 ms on same hardware. For Mistral-X-large we saw slightly better throughput but higher memory pressure when quantized to Q4
[03:40] Samir: quick note on the Mistral results — we saw kernel-level memory fragmentation when mixing Q4 kernels and F16 kernels, subtle but increases tail latency on heavy concurrency
[04:10] Priya: memory fragmentation — any mitigation? we have bursty traffic during business hours so tail is important
[04:30] Jenna: two mitigations: 1) isolate Q4 workloads on dedicated pools (we can do routing policy to flag quantized models), 2) kernel pre-allocation heuristics in the runtime we can enable for Dedicated clusters to avoid fragmentation on bursts
[05:05] Alex: ok, that sounds promising. let's talk MoE — we're experimenting with a sparse 128-expert setup, and routing costs killed our cost model last quarter
[05:30] Samir: right — MoE routing cost depends on router entropy and token affinity. if tokens scatter across many experts you pay cross-GPU comms. What we recommend is token-affinity heuristics to bias routing towards locality and a small sticky-routing window so repeating tokens reuse expert assignments
[06:05] Jenna: also consider hybrid routing: deterministic affinity for top-k tokens and fallback to entropy-based routing for novelty. In practice, that reduced cross-device all-to-all by ~42% in our internal tests on code-gen workloads
[06:45] Marcus (Heliodor): is that something we can configure per-route? our product needs different routing for conversations vs embedding generation
[07:00] Samir: yes, Redwood routing policies are per-route. You can pin conversation routes to low-entropy sticky affinity and use more exploratory routing for offline batch jobs
[07:25] Alex: how does ROPE scaling interplay with MoE routing? we saw drift when using rope scaling for long context which seemed to change token distribution across experts over long sessions
[07:50] Jenna: great observation — ROPE scaling (decay/scale adjustments) can shift attention patterns; that in turn changes router inputs and can cause expert churn. We recommend two things: 1) calibrate ROPE scale so that positional embeddings remain within the router's expected distribution, 2) run a rolling warm start where you let the router adapt during an initial warmup period instead of cold-switching weights
[08:30] Samir: practically, on Heliodor-style RAG flows with 10k tokens we found that reducing ROPE scale by ~0.8 and enabling a 500-token sticky window cut expert churn by half and reduced cross-GPU traffic noticeably
[09:05] Priya: curious about KV prewarm — our sessions have many short-lived chats; prewarmed KV helps but consumes memory, how do we balance that?
[09:30] Jenna: two levers: prefix-based shared KV caching for common system prompts (low memory) and short-lived per-session KV shards for active sessions. Also consider LRU eviction tuned to session length distribution — if your median session is 18 tokens, you can be aggressive on eviction
[10:10] Alex: do you support KV-shard affinity across GPUs? we want minimal cross-shard fetching
[10:28] Jenna: yes, KV-shard affinity is supported. You can configure affinity either by session ID hashing or by conversation owner. For bursty workloads we recommend hashing with hot-key replication for the top 5% of sessions to avoid hot-spot misses
[10:55] Samir: moving to quant: we ran Q4 and Q8 across the models. Q4 reduced memory by ~45% but cost quality on small-context summarization tasks unless we did compensated dequantization at logits time
[11:30] Alex: "compensated dequantization" — can you expand?
[11:40] Jenna: sure: instead of naively dequantizing during matmul, we apply a small learned scale vector at output (post-layer) to reduce distribution shift introduced by Q4. It's cheap and recovered about 70% of the quality loss in our internal tests on Llama-like models
[12:05] Priya: does that add latency? we're tight on p99
[12:20] Jenna: negligible — a couple of microseconds per token because it's vectorized on GPU. The tradeoff was worth it for non-critical generation; for high-SLA routes you can stick to Q8 or mixed precision
[12:45] Marcus:what about cost modelling for dedicated vs hosted?
[12:55] Samir: for predictable throughput, Dedicated with reserved pools often wins unit cost when utilization > 60% and for high concurrency MoE workloads because you avoid cross-tenant noisy neighbors and can tune kernels. Hosted is better for variable or low utilization use-cases
[13:20] Alex: do you have a quick rule of thumb for GPU sizing for our expected 250 QPS ephemeral chat ops?
[13:35] Jenna: depends on model mix — for a Mistral+Qwen blend with 512-token median generation, estimated Dedicated sizing: 4x H100-style nodes with autoscaling headroom to 6 nodes. We'll provide a spreadsheet with sensitivity to traffic and batch sizes
[14:05] Samir: quick interruption, there might be a few transcription hiccups in the auto-summary; feel free to correct anything we say after we send notes
[14:20] Alex: ok — when you say 4x H100, is that per-region? we need geo-failover for EU and NA
[14:35] Samir: yes, we'd recommend at least dual-region Dedicated pools and then smart routing across regions. Redwood can replicate model artifacts and optionally warm KV across regions for cold-starts but there is a cost tradeoff
[15:00] Priya: warm KV across regions — latency vs cost, can we do warm on-demand if a few sessions spike in EU?
[15:20] Jenna: yes, adaptive prewarm is an option: we track hot prefixes and prewarm only when a threshold is crossed, that reduces idle memory costs but increases first-request latency slightly
[16:00] Marcus: let's dig into a concrete profiling plan — can Redwood run kernel traces on our dedicated trial and share flamegraphs?
[16:18] Samir: absolutely, we'll run nvprof/NVIDIA Nsight traces and our runtime's internal GC/fragmentation logs. Jenna will correlate traces to per-token latency and highlight hot kernels
[16:40] Jenna: remind me which models you're most concerned about?
[16:50] Alex: Llama-70B-ish family (sharded), Mistral-X-large, and a custom Qwen-compat adapter we maintain for finetuned policies
[17:05] Jenna: ok good, for the sharded 70B we should also look at KV-shard placement and memory compaction intervals — too-frequent compaction increases latency, too-infrequent increases fragmentation and OOM risk
[17:35] Alex: can Redwood tune compaction windows automatically?
[17:45] Jenna: yes, the runtime can auto-tune compaction based on memory pressure heuristics if you enable the experimental memory manager on Dedicated
[18:05] Priya: what about observability — we want token-level cost attribution and traceability for compliance reviews
[18:20] Samir: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and trace hooks you can export to your SIEM. For compliance we'll provide audit logs and KMS-wrapped keys for encryption at rest
[18:50] Marcus: SOC2, ISO — where are you on certification?
[19:00] Samir: Redwood is SOC2 Type II and pursuing ISO currently — we'll send the cert pack and the security whitepaper after the call
[19:22] Alex: earlier you mentioned sticky routing window; is that implemented in the open API or is it Redwood-managed?
[19:35] Jenna: it's a routing policy parameter you can set per-route in the Console or via the API — we have both declarative and SDK support
[20:00] Alex: good. on quantization — will you share test harnesses so we can run local A/B with our finetuned Qwen adapter?
[20:18] Jenna: yes we'll share the quant-profile harness and the baseline eval scripts. If you run them we can review results and propose dequantization scales tuned to your distribution
[20:40] Priya: given our VPC peering constraint, any additional networking requirements?
[20:55] Samir: aside from peering, ensure that the peered CIDRs are stable and that you allow our health-check IP range; for on-prem we also need an outbound tunnel for the control plane unless you choose fully air-gapped Private deployment
[21:20] Alex: fully air-gapped is hard for us, we'll do VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for now
[21:35] Jenna: noted. ok, quick dive into a micro case: we ran a test where a long RAG session produced attention drift after 6k tokens; with default ROPE we saw top-1 attention shift and that caused router instability
[21:55] Alex: was that on MoE?
[22:02] Jenna: yes, MoE plus ROPE drift amplified router entropy — our mitigation was to apply a small negative decay to ROPE (0.02 per 1k tokens) and a sticky routing multiplier; this kept attention anchors stable and reduced expert flips
[22:30] Marcus: curious whether that affects generation quality downsteam — anything degraded?
[22:45] Jenna: minimal quality impact in our A/B; the token ordering remained coherent because the ROPE change is subtle, but we did re-run logits calibration after adjusting ROPE to be safe
[23:10] Alex: re: batching — earlier you said batching of 8 reduced latency but increased p99 — is there a recommended max batch to avoid tail impact?
[23:30] Jenna: for interactive chat we rarely batch above 6 for Llama-2-13B-class models; for Mistral and Qwen you can push to 8-12 depending on desired p50 vs p99 tradeoff. Dedicated lets you shape batching per-route so you can have low-latency routes with small batches and background scoring with large batches
[24:00] Priya: on the Dedicated trial, can we get both options enabled? low-latency pool + high-throughput pool?
[24:15] Samir: yes, that's our standard pattern: dual pools with autoscaling rules and smart routing policies between them. We'll provision the recommended sizing and tune after the first week of traces
[25:00] Alex: what about the model rollout policy — we need canary and instant rollback when a change causes latency regressions
[25:15] Jenna: Redwood supports canary deploys with traffic weighting and automatic rollback thresholds based on p99 and error rate. We also have shadowing for evaluation without impacting production traffic
[25:40] Marcus: for the POC, we'd like the following measurable success criteria: p99 < 350ms for our median 128-token generation on conversation routes, cost per 1k tokens below our threshold, and no cross-region tail > 800ms for failover paths
[26:05] Samir: those sound reasonable; we'll put them into the POC SLA and instrument the Console dashboards accordingly
[26:30] Alex: one more technical: can you show how to capture KV-miss traces correlated with router decisions? we want to see if routing changes cause cache churn
[26:50] Jenna: yes the runtime logs include a KV event stream with a correlation id you can attach to traces. We'll share an example trace where a router decision triggered a KV prefetch and you can see the delta in the flamegraph
[27:20] Samir: taking us into logistics — Jenna will send the microbenchmark CSV and the profiler instructions; Samir will spin up the Dedicated trial and Samir will loop in Billing for PO template
[27:35] Priya: quick question — will Dedicated trial give us full control over kernel flags? we sometimes need to toggle cuBLAS kernels for perf experiments
[27:48] Jenna: yes, Dedicated gives you controlled kernel flag toggles via a restricted set of runtime feature flags; for sensitive flags we require an approved experiment ticket but it's doable
[28:10] Alex: let's agree on a timeline: we want trial by week of Jan 4, profiling session Jan 5. Does that work?
[28:22] Samir: yes, should be fine — I'll request capacity and Jenna will share the run-book
[28:35] Marcus: ok good. any other risks we should call out?
[28:45] Jenna: biggest unknowns are the finetuned Qwen adapter behavior under Q4 and the 70B sharded compaction heuristics, both of which we'll validate in the first 72 hours of the trial and revert to Q8 or adjust compaction if needed
[29:10] Alex: makes sense. can you email the list of default runtime flags you enable on Dedicated?
[29:20] Samir: yes, we'll include that in the onboarding pack
[29:32] --- (longer technical exchange, mid-call profiling notes and ambient talk) ---
[40:00] Jenna: (screen share) here's a quick flamegraph from a Mistral Q4 run — you can see the matmul kernels dominate, but there's a secondary spike from memory alloc/free calls which lines up with the fragmentation note earlier
[41:15] Alex: is that visible in your GC logs?
[41:22] Jenna: yep, we correlated allocation histograms with the tail. The recommendation was to bump the preallocation and enable compaction thresholds during off-peak to reduce fragmentation during peak
[42:10] Priya: we may need to schedule an overnight compaction window then, during our off-peak maintenance window, does Redwood support scheduled compaction?
[42:25] Jenna: yes, can be scheduled via the Console or automations API
[43:00] Samir: circling back to MoE cost — if you can't bias routing sufficiently, there is also a strategy to shard experts by semantics (e.g., topic-based experts) which reduces router entropy but requires offline clustering of prompts
[43:30] Alex: offline clustering — sounds like a data engineering effort, but probably doable
[43:45] Jenna: we'll provide tooling to bootstrap the clusters using your prompt corpus and show the expected reduction in cross-device traffic
[44:05] Marcus: about failure modes — if a hotspot expert gets overwhelmed, what's the graceful degradation?
[44:20] Samir: the runtime can do expert-level shed — route a fraction of traffic to a dense fallback model instance so you preserve availability and avoid global slowdowns
[44:40] Alex: good. on the billing side, will MoE cross-gpu comms show up as a separate line item?
[44:55] Samir: yes, we break down token cost into compute, memory, and interconnect/egress-like factors in the Console so you can see the hit from cross-device all-to-all
[45:15] Priya: any recommended initial experiments to run during week 1?
[45:30] Jenna: yes — run: 1) cold->warm KV latencies for top 100 prefixes, 2) Q4 vs Q8 A/B on a small finetuned subset, 3) MoE sticky window ablation (0 vs 500 tokens vs 2k tokens), 4) ROPE scale sweep (0.9-1.1) with your representative RAG prompts
[46:10] Alex: can you put those in a checklist? makes it easier to track
[46:20] Samir: will do. we'll also attach expected pass/fail thresholds per test
[46:35] Marcus: last question — is there any reason we couldn't start with a hosted pilot for a few routes while the Dedicated pool is provisioned?
[46:50] Samir: you can, but hosted won't give you the kernel-level toggles or guaranteed isolation. It's fine for early feature testing, but for MoE cost experiments we recommend Dedicated
[47:10] Priya: understood. Then POC plan: spin Dedicated trial, run week-1 experiments, hold kernel trace session Jan 5, and handshake on SLA metrics.
[47:25] Samir: captured. we'll send a calendar invite with the profiling session details
[47:38] Alex: thanks — a couple of small items: 1) we'll share our prompt distribution CSV, 2) we want a small hook in the SDK to tag sessions for KV-affinity testing
[47:55] Jenna: SDK hook is trivial — we can add a session_affinity tag in the client and show mapping in the Console
[48:10] Marcus: great. Any other blockers?
[48:20] Alex: none from engineering beyond getting access to the trial nodes
[48:30] Samir: ok closing with a quick recap: deliverables from Redwood: microbenchmark CSV, profiler run-book, Dedicated trial provisioning, SOC2/security pack. Customers will provide prompt sets, network peering details, and PO to get trial billing squared away
[48:55] Jenna: and we'll set up the Jan 5 profiling session and share the example flamegraphs and KV-correlated traces beforehand
[49:10] Marcus: thanks all — this was helpful
[49:20] Samir: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifact links and owners
[49:30] (call ends)

- Q4 is memory-efficient but needs compensated dequantization to preserve small-context quality
- Kernel fragmentation on mixed-precision workloads is a real tail risk; Dedicated prealloc and compaction scheduling recommended
